title: Erdős Problem #467: Dual Covering by Prime Residue Classes
description: For large x, can we choose residue classes for primes ≤ x and partition them into A ⊔ B so every n < x is covered by both A and B? Related to covering congruences and the Erdős–Graham framework.

meta.author: Erdős, Graham
references: Erdős & Graham (1980): 'Old and New Problems and Results in Combinatorial Number Theory', Enseign. Math. Monograph 28, p. 93
Mertens (1874): 'Ein Beitrag zur analytischen Zahlentheorie', J. Reine Angew. Math. 78, pp. 46–62
Halberstam & Roth (1966): 'Sequences', Oxford University Press — covering congruence framework
Erdős (1950): 'On integers of the form 2^k + p and some related problems', Summa Brasil. Math. 2, pp. 113–123
Filaseta, Ford, Konyagin, Pomerance & Yu (2007): 'Sieving by large integers and covering systems of congruences', J. Amer. Math. Soc. 20, pp. 495–517

overview.historicalContext: Paul Erdős and Ronald Graham posed this problem in their 1980 monograph 'Old and New Problems and Results in Combinatorial Number Theory' (p. 93), within their systematic study of covering congruence systems. The problem builds on Erdős's foundational 1950 work showing that certain integers of the form $2^k + p$ relate to covering systems, and connects to the broader Erdős–Selfridge conjecture on covering systems with distinct moduli. The original formulation has notoriously ambiguous quantifiers — it is unclear whether the residue assignment is fixed or depends on $x$, and whether the partition adapts to the assignment. The Chinese Remainder Theorem provides the key independence tool: for distinct primes, residue class memberships are independent events. Franz Mertens' 1874 third theorem ($\prod_{p \leq x}(1-1/p) \sim e^{-\gamma}/\log x$) quantifies the total prime coverage capacity. The problem asks whether this capacity, growing as $\log\log x$, can be split into two halves each sufficient for complete coverage — a question at the interface of combinatorial number theory, sieve theory, and probabilistic arguments.
overview.problemStatement: For all sufficiently large $x$, do there exist residue classes $a_p$ for each prime $p \leq x$ and a partition $\{p \leq x : p \text{ prime}\} = A \sqcup B$ (both non-empty) such that every $n < x$ satisfies $n \equiv a_p \pmod{p}$ for some $p \in A$ and $n \equiv a_q \pmod{q}$ for some $q \in B$?
overview.proofStrategy: We formalize the core objects — residue assignments as dependent functions, prime partitions as Boolean classifiers with non-emptiness witnesses, and dual coverage as a universal-existential proposition. We prove basic properties of residue classes (periodicity, density $1/p$, single coverage by smallest prime factor), analyze the zero assignment (covers all $n \geq 2$ but not $n = 1$), derive structural constraints on dual coverings (each half covers independently, double-hit property, $x \geq 2$ requirement), and axiomatize the CRT and Mertens' estimate as the analytical backbone.
keyInsights: **Single coverage is trivial, dual is hard**: Every $n \geq 2$ has a prime factor $\leq n$, so one set of all primes trivially covers $[2, x)$. The challenge is splitting primes into two halves each achieving full coverage independently

**CRT independence makes coverage multiplicative**: For distinct primes, the probability a random integer avoids all residue classes in a set $S$ is $\prod_{p \in S}(1 - 1/p)$, turning the coverage problem into a product estimate

**Mertens' theorem bounds the budget**: $\prod_{p \leq x}(1 - 1/p) \sim e^{-\gamma}/\log x \to 0$, but splitting this product into two parts requires each sub-product to also vanish — feasible only if both halves capture enough of $\sum 1/p \sim \log\log x$

**Small primes dominate the allocation**: Prime 2 covers half the integers, 3 covers a third, etc. Assigning $p = 2$ to one side forces the other to cover all even integers from odd primes alone — a severe constraint showing small primes must be shared carefully

**Ambiguous quantifiers create multiple problems**: The original [ErGr80] formulation is unclear on whether $\alpha$ is universal or existential. The strongest reading (fixed $\alpha$ works for all partitions) is likely false; the weakest (both $\alpha$ and partition depend on $x$) is the formalized version

sections.title: Header, Docstring, and Imports
sections.summary: Module docstring referencing [ErGr80, p. 93] with the full problem statement and OPEN status. Imports `Mathlib.Data.Nat.Prime.Basic` for primality and `Mathlib.Tactic` for proof automation.

sections.title: Core Definitions: Assignment, Partition, Coverage
sections.summary: Four definitions: `ResidueAssignment` ($\alpha : \{p \leq x\} \to \mathbb{N}$), `PrimePartition` ($A \sqcup B$ with non-emptiness), `CoveredByA`/`CoveredByB` ($n \equiv a_p \pmod{p}$ for some $p$ in the respective set), and `IsDualCovering` (conjunction of both coverages for all $n < x$).

sections.title: The Main Conjecture (OPEN)
sections.summary: Erdős Problem #467 axiomatized: $\exists X, \forall x \geq X, \exists \alpha, \exists A \sqcup B: \text{IsDualCovering}(x, \alpha, A \sqcup B)$. The existential threshold $X$ allows finitely many exceptions.

sections.title: Basic Properties of Residue Classes
sections.summary: Six proved lemmas: $n \bmod p < p$, zero class $\iff$ divisibility, even-or-odd dichotomy, periodicity ($n + kp \equiv n$), existence of prime factors for $n \geq 2$, and prime factor bounded by $x$ for $n < x$.

sections.title: Covering by Zero Residue Classes
sections.summary: Analysis of the zero assignment $\alpha \equiv 0$: covers $n = 0$ trivially, fails at $n = 1$ (no prime divides 1), covers all $n \geq 2$ via smallest prime factor. The `zeroAssignment` definition and its characterization $p \mid n \iff$ covered.

sections.title: Partition and Dual Covering Constraints
sections.summary: Structural theorems: dual covering implies each half covers independently, the **double hit** property ($\exists p \in A, q \in B$ covering $n$), partition uses $\geq 2$ primes, distinct labels exist, and $x \geq 2$ is necessary.

sections.title: Residue Class Periodicity and Counting
sections.summary: Three lemmas: periodicity $(n + p) \bmod p = n \bmod p$, identity $a \bmod p = a$ for $a < p$, and the count $n \bmod p < p$ establishing exactly $p$ residue classes mod $p$.

sections.title: CRT and Mertens Axioms
sections.summary: Two axiomatized results: the **Chinese Remainder Theorem** for distinct primes ($\exists n: n \equiv a \pmod{p} \wedge n \equiv b \pmod{q}$) and **Mertens' third theorem** ($\prod_{p \leq x}(1 - 1/p) \sim e^{-\gamma}/\log x$).

sections.title: Problem Summary
sections.summary: Records OPEN status and restates the fundamental observation: every $n \geq 2$ has a prime factor, making single coverage trivial. The theorem `coverage_exceeds_target` confirms single-set sufficiency.

conclusion.summary: This formalization captures the full structure of Erdős Problem #467: the dual covering requirement, the interplay between residue assignments and prime partitions, structural constraints derived from the partition, and the analytical tools (CRT independence, Mertens' product estimate) that govern coverage capacity. The 242-line file proves all elementary properties while axiomatizing the deep results (CRT, Mertens) and the main conjecture itself.
conclusion.implications: A resolution would advance the theory of covering congruence systems, clarifying whether the prime coverage capacity ($\sum 1/p \sim \log\log x$) can be halved while maintaining completeness. This connects to sieve theory (Brun, Selberg), the Erdős–Selfridge conjecture on odd covering systems, and the general question of how efficiently prime moduli can tile the integers.
openQuestions: Does a dual covering exist for all sufficiently large $x$, or are there infinitely many $x$ where no partition works?
What is the role of the residue assignment: does the zero assignment plus careful partition suffice, or are non-trivial assignments essential?
How does the minimum threshold $X$ depend on the partition structure — is $X$ polynomial or exponential in the number of primes?
Can the problem be generalized to $k$-fold coverings ($k \geq 3$), and how does the feasibility threshold scale with $k$?
